title: Conjecture 1.8
context_text: A subdivision of a multigraph $H$ is a graph obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path of length at least one between $u$ and $v$, these paths being internally disjoint; a graph $G$ is $H$-subdivision-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $H$. For an integer $\rho\ge0$, $\chi^{\rho}(G)$ is the maximum over all vertices $v$ of the chromatic number of the subgraph induced on the set $N^{\rho}[v]$ of vertices at distance at most $\rho$ from $v$. An ideal is a class of graphs closed under taking induced subgraphs; it is colourable if its members have bounded chromatic number, and $\rho$-bounded if $\chi^{\rho}(G)\le\tau$ for some $\tau$ and all its members. A multigraph $H$ is widespread if for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ there is $\rho\ge0$ such that every $\rho$-bounded ideal of $J$-subdivision-free graphs is colourable, i.e. for all $\tau$ there is $c$ such that every $J$-subdivision-free graph $G$ with $\chi^{\rho}(G)\le\tau$ has $\chi(G)\le c$. $H$ is pervasive in a class $\mathcal{C}$ if for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ and every $\kappa$ there is $c$ such that every $J$-subdivision-free $G\in\mathcal{C}$ with clique number at most $\kappa$ has $\chi(G)\le c$. Scott conjectured that every multigraph is pervasive in the class of all graphs, which was disproved by Pawlik, Kozik, Krawczyk, Lasoń, Micek, Trotter and Walczak; only forests of chandeliers can be pervasive there (a chandelier is a tree plus a new vertex, the pivot, adjacent to its leaves; a forest of chandeliers is built by repeatedly gluing chandeliers at their pivots, component by component), and forests of chandeliers are pervasive in every controlled ideal (one in which, for some $\rho$, every $\rho$-bounded subideal is colourable). The authors originally expected the widespread multigraphs to be exactly the forests of chandeliers, but in this paper they prove that every multigraph obtained from a tree by replacing edges with bundles of parallel edges (a banana tree) is widespread, and give widespread graphs that are not forests of chandeliers; this conjecture is their resuscitated version of Scott's conjecture. They are very far from proving it: they do not know whether every chandelier is widespread, and all multigraphs proved widespread so far are subdivisions of outerplanar graphs.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. VI. Banana trees

title: Conjecture 1.10
statement_text: For all graphs $J$ and for all integers $\tau \geq 0$, there exists $c$ such that if $G$ is a graph with chromatic number more than $c$, then either some induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $J$ or $\chi^2(G) > \tau$.
context_text: A subdivision of a multigraph $H$ is a graph obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path of length at least one between $u$ and $v$, these paths being internally disjoint; a graph $G$ is $H$-subdivision-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $H$. $\chi^{2}(G)$ is the maximum, over all vertices $v$ of $G$, of the chromatic number of the subgraph induced on the set of vertices at distance at most $2$ from $v$ (more generally $\chi^{\rho}(G)$ uses distance at most $\rho$). So the conjecture says that graphs of huge chromatic number either contain an induced subdivision of $J$ or contain a ball of radius $2$ with large chromatic number. A multigraph $H$ is widespread if for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ there is $\rho$ such that for all $\tau$ there is $c$ with $\chi(G)\le c$ for every $J$-subdivision-free graph $G$ with $\chi^{\rho}(G)\le\tau$; the authors conjecture that every multigraph is widespread (a resuscitated version of Scott's disproved conjecture). Using their result with Chudnovsky that, for all $\rho\ge2$ and every multigraph $J$, every $\rho$-controlled class of $J$-subdivision-free graphs is $2$-controlled (an ideal is $\rho$-controlled if each of its subideals with bounded $\chi^{\rho}$ has bounded chromatic number), they show that this conjecture is equivalent to the statement that every multigraph is widespread, and present it as a nicer reformulation (not used in the paper). In this paper they prove that every tree with edges replaced by bundles of parallel edges is widespread.

title: Open Question: first pervasiveness characterisation
statement_text: Which multigraphs $H$ have the property that for all $\kappa$ there exists $c$ such that every $H$-subdivision-free graph with clique number at most $\kappa$ has chromatic number at most $c$?
context_text: A subdivision of a multigraph $H$ is a graph obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path of length at least one between $u$ and $v$, these paths being internally disjoint; a graph $G$ is $H$-subdivision-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $H$. The question asks for which multigraphs $H$ the class of $H$-subdivision-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded in the weak sense that bounded clique number implies bounded chromatic number. The authors contrast it with a second question: for which $H$ does this hold for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ in place of $H$ (i.e. graphs of bounded clique number and huge chromatic number contain an induced subdivision of $H$ in which every edge is subdivided at least a prescribed number of times); $H$ is then called pervasive. They find the second question perhaps better: when restricted to controlled classes (ideals in which large chromatic number forces a ball of bounded radius with large chromatic number) its answer is known (forests of chandeliers, i.e. trees of chandeliers glued at pivots, are pervasive in every controlled ideal, and only they can be pervasive in all graphs, by work of Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour), whereas the first question remains open. Scott conjectured that every multigraph is pervasive in the class of all graphs, which was disproved; the authors prove that multigraphs obtained from a tree by adding parallel edges are pervasive in the class of all graphs.
